arXiv:2407.09272v2 [math.GR] 19 Sep 2025

Residually rationally solvable one-relator groups

Marco Linton Address: Instituto de Ciencias Matemáticas, CSIC-UAM-UC3M-UCM, Madrid, Spain Email address: marco.linton@icmat.es
Abstract.

We show that the intersection of the rational derived series of a one-relator group is rationally perfect and is normally generated by a single element. As a corollary, we characterise precisely when a one-relator group is residually rationally solvable.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
20E26, 20F14, 20F05

1. Introduction

If GG is a group, the subgroup

Gℚ(i):={g|gk∈[Gℚ(i−1),Gℚ(i−1)],k≠0}⊴G,G^{(i)}_{\mathbb{Q}}:=\left\{g\bigm|g^{k}\in\left[G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(i-1)},G^{(i-1)}_{\mathbb{Q}}\right],\,k\neq 0\right\}\trianglelefteq G,

is the ithi^{\text{th}} term of the rational derived series, with Gℚ(0)=GG^{(0)}_{\mathbb{Q}}=G. It is so denoted as Gℚ(i)G^{(i)}_{\mathbb{Q}} is the kernel of the natural map to the first homology group of Gℚ(i−1)G^{(i-1)}_{\mathbb{Q}} over the rationals. A group GG is rationally solvable (or ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable) if Gℚ(n)=1G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(n)}=1 for some nn and is residually rationally solvable if

Gℚ(ω):=⋂i=0∞Gℚ(i)=1.G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(\omega)}:=\bigcap_{i=0}^{\infty}G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(i)}=1.

The (rational) derived series can be continued to form the transcendental (rational) derived series. The intersection of all terms of the (rational) transcendental derived series is the maximal (rationally) perfect subgroup of GG.

Baumslag proved in [Bau71] that all positive one-relator groups, that is, groups with a single defining relation that do not mention any inverse generators, are residually solvable; or in other words, they have G(ω)=1G^{(\omega)}=1. Our main theorem computes Gℚ(ω)G^{(\omega)}_{\mathbb{Q}} for all one-relator groups and generalises Baumslag’s result.

Theorem 1.1.

Let FF be a free group, w∈Fw\in F a word and G=F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle a one-relator group. There is a word r∈Fr\in F, of length bounded above by that of ww, and an integer k⩾1k\geqslant 1 such that w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle] and

Gℚ(ω+1)=Gℚ(ω)=⟨⟨r⟩⟩G.G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(\omega+1)}=G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(\omega)}=\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G}.

In particular, the maximal residually rationally solvable quotient of GG is the one-relator group F/⟨⟨r⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle.

Torsion-free one-relator groups cannot contain finitely generated rationally perfect subgroups since they are locally indicable by a result of Brodskii [Bro84] (see also Howie [How82]) and so the subgroup Gℚ(ω)G^{(\omega)}_{\mathbb{Q}} from Theorem 1.1 is always infinitely generated when it is non-trivial. The prototypical examples of non residually (rationally) solvable one-relator groups are the Baumslag–Gersten groups [Bau69]:

G(1,n)≅⟨a,t∣[at,a]=an−1⟩.G(1,n)\cong\langle a,t\mid[a^{t},a]=a^{n-1}\rangle.

Here we adopt the convention that at=t−1​a​ta^{t}=t^{-1}at and [at,a]=at​a​(at)−1​a−1[a^{t},a]=a^{t}a(a^{t})^{-1}a^{-1}. When n≠1n\neq 1, the relator expresses (a power of) aa as a commutator over itself and a conjugate of itself. Thus, the normal closure of aa is perfect when n=2n=2 and is rationally perfect (has torsion abelianisation) otherwise. Theorem 1.1 says that the maximal rationally perfect subgroup of any one-relator group is essentially always of this form; that is, the normal closure of a single element that can be read off from the relator. In fact, it is worth pointing out that in general, if G=F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle is a one-relator group, k⩾1k\geqslant 1 and w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle], then ⟨⟨r⟩⟩G\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G} is a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-perfect subgroup of GG.

If GG is a one-relator group with H2​(G)=0H^{2}(G)=0, then a result of Strebel [Str74] implies that G(α)=Gℚ(α)G^{(\alpha)}=G^{(\alpha)}_{\mathbb{Q}} for all ordinals α\alpha. Thus, Theorem 1.1 is also true for the ordinary derived series of one-relator groups GG under the additional hypothesis that H2​(G)=0H^{2}(G)=0. We thank Jens Harlander for pointing this out to us. We conjecture that Theorem 1.1 holds also for the derived series of all one-relator groups, with a minor modification, see Conjecture 4.8.

With little work, we obtain a satisfying characterisation of residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable one-relator groups.

Corollary 1.2.

Let FF be a free group, w∈Fw\in F a word and G=F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle a one-relator group. The following are equivalent:

  1. (1)

    GG is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable.

  2. (2)

    Gℚ(n)G^{(n)}_{\mathbb{Q}} is a free group for some integer n⩾0n\geqslant 0.

  3. (3)

    For all words r∈Fr\in F of length at most that of ww, and all integers k⩾1k\geqslant 1, if w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle], then ww is conjugate to rr or r−1r^{-1}.

The equivalence between (1) and (2) is a consequence of Theorem 3.2, a key step in the proof of Theorem 1.1. In fact, a consequence of our proofs is that the integer nn from (2) may be taken to be the length of the relator ww. If GG is not residually rationally solvable, then Gℚ(n)G^{(n)}_{\mathbb{Q}} is an extension of the maximal rationally perfect subgroup by a free group.

Using Theorem 1.1, we recover and strengthen Baumslag’s result.

Corollary 1.3.

Torsion-free positive one-relator groups are free-by-(ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable) and so are residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable. Positive one-relator groups with torsion are free-by-solvable and so are residually solvable.

Using Theorem 1.1, we may also algorithmically determine whether a one-relator group is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable or not. In fact, the algorithm computes the element rr from Theorem 1.1. Note that in general it is undecidable whether a finitely presented group is residually rationally solvable.

Corollary 1.4.

There is an algorithm that, on input a word ww over an alphabet S⊔S−1S\sqcup S^{-1}, decides whether the one-relator group F⁡(S)/⟨⟨w⟩⟩F(S)/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable.

It would be interesting to obtain similar characterisations for residually solvable one-relator groups and residually (torsion-free) nilpotent one-relator groups. An intriguing question of Arzhantseva asks whether all one-relator groups are residually amenable [KM18, Problem 18.6]. In light of Theorem 1.1, it would be especially interesting to know whether the Baumslag–Gersten groups are residually amenable.

We conclude this introduction by remarking that this article is almost entirely self-contained: the only results we use and do not prove are old theorems of Magnus on one-relator groups [Mag30, Mag32] and on residual ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvability of free groups [Mag35] and the Burns–Hale Theorem [BH72]. We also take inspiration from Howie’s tower method [How81].

2. Weakly reducible complexes and their regular covers

Throughout this article, a 2-complex will be taken to mean a two-dimensional CW-complex whose attaching maps are given by immersions. All maps between 2-complexes will be assumed to be combinatorial, that is, open nn-cells are sent homeomorphically to open nn-cells. In fact, most maps will just be covering spaces or inclusions.

A weak elementary reduction is a pair of 2-complexes X⊂ZX\subset Z such that Z−XZ-X consists of a single 1-cell and at most one 2-cell whose attaching map traverses the 1-cell. It is an elementary collapse if Z−XZ-X contains a 2-cell whose attaching map traverses the 1-cell precisely once. Note that our definition of a weak elementary reduction is a weak version of Howie’s notion of an elementary reduction from [How82].

If α\alpha is an ordinal number, say a 2-complex ZZ is weakly α\alpha-reducible to XX if there are subcomplexes Xβ⊂ZX_{\beta}\subset Z for each β⩽α\beta\leqslant\alpha such that X0=XX_{0}=X, Xα=ZX_{\alpha}=Z, Xβ−1⊂XβX_{\beta-1}\subset X_{\beta} is a weak elementary reduction for each successor ordinal β\beta and Xβ=⋃γ<βXγX_{\beta}=\bigcup_{\gamma<\beta}X_{\gamma} for each limit ordinal β\beta. Say ZZ is weakly α\alpha-reducible if it is weakly α\alpha-reducible to its 0-skeleton. When α⩽ω\alpha\leqslant\omega, we shall just say that ZZ is weakly reducible or weakly reducible to XX. For locally finite 2-complexes, any weakly α\alpha-reducible 2-complex (to a given subcomplex) is actually weakly reducible (to a given subcomplex).

Lemma 2.1.

Let α\alpha be an ordinal and let ZZ be a 2-complex weakly α\alpha-reducible to X⊂ZX\subset Z. If Z−XZ-X has countably many cells and if each 1-cell in Z−XZ-X is traversed by finitely many attaching maps of 2-cells, then ZZ is weakly reducible to XX.

Proof.

For each ordinal β⩽α\beta\leqslant\alpha, denote by Xβ⊂ZX_{\beta}\subset Z the associated subcomplex. We construct a directed graph Γ\Gamma as follows. The vertices of this graph are the successor ordinals β⩽α\beta\leqslant\alpha and two vertices β\beta and γ\gamma are connected by a directed edge if the following holds:

  1. (1)

    β<γ\beta<\gamma.

  2. (2)

    Xγ−Xγ−1X_{\gamma}-X_{\gamma-1} contains a 2-cell cc.

  3. (3)

    Xβ−Xβ−1X_{\beta}-X_{\beta-1} contains a 1-cell traversed by the attaching map for cc.

Intuitively, we are encoding the dependency between the different weak elementary reductions in the graph Γ\Gamma. Since each 1-cell in Z−XZ-X is traversed by finitely many attaching maps of 2-cells, this directed graph is locally finite. Denote by S⊂V⁡(Γ)S\subset V(\Gamma) the vertices with no incoming edges. If v∈V⁡(Γ)v\in V(\Gamma) is a vertex, denote by Γv⊂Γ\Gamma_{v}\subset\Gamma the union of all directed paths in Γ\Gamma that end at vv. The well-order on the vertices, together with the local finiteness of Γ\Gamma, implies that Γv\Gamma_{v} is finite for all v∈V⁡(Γ)v\in V(\Gamma) as each directed path ending at vv yields a descending chain. Indeed, if Γv\Gamma_{v} was infinite, then the local finiteness of Γ\Gamma implies that there is some edge leading into vv with origin uu such that Γu\Gamma_{u} is infinite. Repeating this, one may find an infinite descending chain, contradicting the well-ordering on the vertices. Furthermore, the well-ordering also implies that Γ\Gamma is acyclic. Denote by depth⁡(v)\depth(v) the maximal length of a directed path in Γv\Gamma_{v}, which is well-defined since Γ\Gamma is acyclic, and by roots⁡(v)⊂S\roots(v)\subset S the set of vertices in Γv\Gamma_{v} that have no incoming edges.

Choose any injection ϕ:S→ℕ\phi\colon S\to\mathbb{N}. We extend ϕ\phi to a map ϕ¯:V⁡(Γ)→ℕ\bar{\phi}\colon V(\Gamma)\to\mathbb{N} by defining

ϕ¯(v)=min{k∣depth(v)⩽k,roots(v)⊂ϕ−1({0,…,k−1})}.\bar{\phi}(v)=\min{\{k\mid\depth(v)\leqslant k,\roots(v)\subset\phi^{-1}(\{0,\ldots,k-1\})\}}.

Since Γ\Gamma is locally finite, ϕ¯\bar{\phi} is a finite to one map.

For each successor ordinal β⩽α\beta\leqslant\alpha, denote by cβ=Xβ−Xβ−1c_{\beta}=X_{\beta}-X_{\beta-1}, which is either a 1-cell or a 1-cell and a 2-cell. Now define Z0=XZ_{0}=X and

Zl+1=Zl∪⋃β∈ϕ¯−1​(l+1)cβ.Z_{l+1}=Z_{l}\cup\bigcup_{\beta\in\bar{\phi}^{-1}(l+1)}c_{\beta}.

By definition of ϕ¯\bar{\phi}, we have that Zl+1Z_{l+1} actually weakly kk-reduces to ZlZ_{l} where k=|ϕ¯−1​(l+1)|<∞k=|\bar{\phi}^{-1}(l+1)|<\infty and Z=⋃i=0∞ZiZ=\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}Z_{i}. Thus, ZZ weakly reduces to XX. ∎

Finite sheeted covers of weakly reducible complexes are almost never themselves weakly reducible. Howie took advantage of the fact that infinite cyclic covers of weakly reducible complexes are weakly reducible in [How82]. We here generalise this fact to locally indicable covers.

Proposition 2.2.

Let ZZ be a 2-complex weakly reducible to XX, such that Z−XZ-X contains countably many 2-cells and each 1-cell in Z−XZ-X is traversed by finitely many attaching maps of 2-cells. If p:Y→Zp\colon Y\to Z is a regular cover with Deck⁡(p)\deck(p) locally indicable, then YY is weakly reducible to p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X).

Proof.

Express ZZ as a union of weak elementary reductions X=X0⊂X1⊂X2⊂…⊂ZX=X_{0}\subset X_{1}\subset X_{2}\subset\ldots\subset Z. If for each nn, we have that p−1​(Xn+1)p^{-1}(X_{n+1}) is weakly reducible to p−1​(Xn)p^{-1}(X_{n}), then YY will be weakly ω2\omega^{2}-reducible to p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X). By Lemma 2.1, YY will be weakly reducible to p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X). Thus it suffices to prove the result in the case that X⊂ZX\subset Z is a weak elementary reduction. If Z−XZ-X does not contain a 2-cell, then the result is clear, so now suppose that Z−X=e∪cZ-X=e\cup c, where ee is a 1-cell and cc is a 2-cell. If Z1⊂ZZ_{1}\subset Z denotes the closure of cc and X1=X∩Z1X_{1}=X\cap Z_{1}, then X1⊂Z1X_{1}\subset Z_{1} is a weak elementary reduction and if p−1​(Z1)p^{-1}(Z_{1}) weakly reduces to p−1​(X1)p^{-1}(X_{1}), then YY weakly reduces to p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X). Thus, we may assume that ZZ itself is the closure of a single 2-cell and X⊂ZX\subset Z is a weak elementary reduction to a 1-subcomplex.

The proof now proceeds by induction on c⁡(Z)=|λ|−|Z(0)|c(Z)=|\lambda|-|Z^{(0)}|, where λ:S1→Z(1)\lambda\colon S^{1}\to Z^{(1)} denotes the attaching map for cc. Consider the induced epimorphism π1​(Z)→Deck⁡(p)=G\pi_{1}(Z)\to\deck(p)=G. Since ZZ is the closure of a single 2-cell, it is compact and hence GG is finitely generated. Since GG is finitely generated and locally indicable, either G=1G=1, or there is some epimorphism π1​(Z)→ℤ\pi_{1}(Z)\to\mathbb{Z} factoring through an epimorphism G→ℤG\to\mathbb{Z}. In the first case there is nothing to prove so, let us assume that we are in the second case. Let K→ZK\to Z be the induced ℤ\mathbb{Z}-cover. By construction, π1​(Y)⩽ker⁡(π1​(Z)→ℤ)=π1​(K)\pi_{1}(Y)\leqslant\ker(\pi_{1}(Z)\to\mathbb{Z})=\pi_{1}(K) and so Y→ZY\to Z factors as a composition of covers Y→K→ZY\to K\to Z. Denote by q:Y→Kq\colon Y\to K.

If e0⊂Ke_{0}\subset K is a lift of ee, denote by ei=ti⋅e0e_{i}=t^{i}\cdot e_{0}, where tt is a generator of the deck group of K→ZK\to Z. Denote by D⊂KD\subset K the closure of some lift of cc. Then let mm be the minimal integer and MM the maximal such that em,eM⊂De_{m},e_{M}\subset D. Since DD surjects ZZ, we have c⁡(D)⩽c⁡(Z)c(D)\leqslant c(Z). Since c⁡(D)=c⁡(Z)c(D)=c(Z) if and only if D→ZD\to Z is an isomorphism, it follows that c⁡(D)<c⁡(Z)c(D)<c(Z). The pairs D(1)−eM=L⊂DD^{(1)}-e_{M}=L\subset D and D(1)−em=U⊂DD^{(1)}-e_{m}=U\subset D are both weak elementary reductions.

Now consider the subcomplexes

D−1\displaystyle D_{-1} =q​(p−1​(X)),\displaystyle=q(p^{-1}(X)),
D0\displaystyle D_{0} =D−1∪D,\displaystyle=D_{-1}\cup D,
Di+1\displaystyle D_{i+1} =Di∪t−i−1⋅D∪ti+1⋅D,∀i⩾0.\displaystyle=D_{i}\cup t^{-i-1}\cdot D\cup t^{i+1}\cdot D,\qquad\forall i\geqslant 0.

By the inductive hypothesis, q−1​(ti⋅D)q^{-1}(t^{i}\cdot D) weakly reduces to q−1​(ti⋅L)q^{-1}(t^{i}\cdot L) and to q−1​(ti⋅U)q^{-1}(t^{i}\cdot U) for all i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}. Thus we see that q−1​(Di+1)q^{-1}(D_{i+1}) weakly reduces to q−1​(Di)q^{-1}(D_{i}) for all i⩾−1i\geqslant-1. But then q−1​(K)=Yq^{-1}(K)=Y weakly ω2\omega^{2}-reduces to q−1​(D−1)=p−1​(X)q^{-1}(D_{-1})=p^{-1}(X) and so YY weakly reduces to p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X) by Lemma 2.1 as claimed. ∎

3. Separating elements in locally indicable quotients

The following theorem is a classical result due to Weinbaum [Wei72].

Theorem 3.1 (Weinbaum’s Theorem).

If FF is a free group, w∈Fw\in F is a word and G=F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle is a one-relator group, then every proper non-empty subword of ww is non-trivial in GG.

Howie generalised Theorem 3.1 in [How82] to one-relator products of locally indicable groups. We here show that if this property holds in a locally indicable quotient of an arbitrary one-relator product, then the kernel admits a particularly nice decomposition as a free product. This will yield consequences for the residual properties of one-relator groups.

Theorem 3.2.

Let AA and BB be countable groups, let n⩾1n\geqslant 1 be an integer, let w∈A∗Bw\in A*B be a cyclically reduced word of length at least two that is not a proper power and consider the one-relator product G=A∗B⟨⟨wn⟩⟩G=\frac{A*B}{\langle\!\langle w^{n}\rangle\!\rangle}. If ϕ:G→Q\phi\colon G\to Q is a homomorphism to a locally indicable group such that ϕ⁡(u)≠1\phi(u)\neq 1 for each proper non-empty subword uu of ww, then ker⁡(ϕ)\ker(\phi) splits as a free product of a free group, subgroups of AA, subgroups of BB and copies of ℤ/n​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

Let XA,XBX_{A},X_{B} be 2-complexes with π1​(XA)=A\pi_{1}(X_{A})=A and π1​(XB)=B\pi_{1}(X_{B})=B, let X=XA⊔XBX=X_{A}\sqcup X_{B} and let ZZ be the 2-complex obtained by attaching a 1-cell ee to XX connecting the two components and attaching a 2-cell cc along an attaching map λ\lambda spelling out the word wnw^{n}. Since ww is cyclically reduced of length at least two, λ\lambda traverses ee and so X⊂ZX\subset Z is a weak elementary reduction with π1​(Z)=G\pi_{1}(Z)=G. A homomorphism ϕ:G→Q\phi\colon G\to Q to a locally indicable group induces a regular cover p:Y→Zp\colon Y\to Z with Deck⁡(p)=im⁡(ϕ)\deck(p)=\Ima(\phi). By Proposition 2.2, YY is weakly reducible to p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X). Since ϕ⁡(u)≠1\phi(u)\neq 1 for each proper non-empty subword of ww, it follows that each lift λ~\tilde{\lambda} of λ\lambda to Y(1)Y^{(1)} factors as

where γ\gamma is an nn-fold cover and where λ~′\tilde{\lambda}^{\prime} traverses each lift of ee at most once. Hence, when n=1n=1, Proposition 2.2 implies that YY is collapsible to a connected subcomplex consisting of p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X) and some lifts of ee. In particular, YY deformation retracts onto a (connected) subcomplex of YY which decomposes as a union of a 1-subcomplex and the components of p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X), whence the conclusion of the theorem. Denote by CnC_{n} the 2-complex with 1-skeleton S1S^{1} and with 2-cell attached along an nn-fold cover S1→S1S^{1}\to S^{1}. If n⩾2n\geqslant 2, then YY is homotopy equivalent to a (connected) subcomplex of YY which decomposes as a union of a 1-subcomplex and the components of p−1​(X)p^{-1}(X), wedged with copies of the 2-complexes CnC_{n}. ∎

If 𝒞\mathcal{C} is any collection of groups, we say that GG is residually 𝒞\mathcal{C} if for every non-trivial element g∈Gg\in G, there is an epimorphism ϕ:G→Q\phi\colon G\to Q with Q∈𝒞Q\in\mathcal{C} such that ϕ⁡(g)≠1\phi(g)\neq 1. We say GG is fully residually 𝒞\mathcal{C} if for every finite set of non-trivial elements S⊂GS\subset G, there is an epimorphism ϕ:G→Q\phi\colon G\to Q with Q∈𝒞Q\in\mathcal{C} such that 1∉ϕ⁡(S)1\notin\phi(S). When 𝒞\mathcal{C} is closed under taking subdirect products, the two notions coincide.

Corollary 3.3.

Let GG be a non-free one-relator group and let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be any collection of locally indicable groups. If GG is fully residually 𝒞\mathcal{C}, then GG has a surjective homomorphism to a group in 𝒞\mathcal{C} whose kernel is free.

Proof.

Firstly, since each group in 𝒞\mathcal{C} is torsion-free, GG must also be torsion-free as elements of finite order lie in the kernel of any homomorphism to a torsion-free group. Let FF be a free group and w∈Fw\in F such that G≅F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G\cong F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle. Since GG is torsion-free and not free, we have that ww is an imprimitve element in some free factor of FF of rank at least two. Thus, we may express F=A∗BF=A*B with A,B≠1A,B\neq 1 and with ww being a (after possibly replacing with a conjugate) cyclically reduced word over A∗BA*B of length at least two that is also not a proper power. By Theorem 3.1, each proper non-empty subword of ww is non-trivial in GG. Since GG is fully residually 𝒞\mathcal{C}, there is some group C∈𝒞C\in\mathcal{C} and an epimorphism ϕ:G→C\phi\colon G\to C such that ϕ⁡(u)≠1\phi(u)\neq 1 for each proper non-empty subword uu of ww. Now we may apply Theorem 3.2 to obtain that ker⁡(ϕ)\ker(\phi) is a free group as required. ∎

Corollary 3.3 applies for instance to residually torsion-free nilpotent, residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable and fully residually free one-relator groups. Since RFRS (which stands for residually finite rationally solvable) groups are (fully) residually virtually abelian and locally indicable [OS24, Theorem 6.3], a fact that Okun–Schreve attribute to Fisher and Kielak, Corollary 3.3 also implies that RFRS one-relator groups are free-by-{virtually abelian locally indicable}.

4. The rational derived series of a one-relator group

We now refine Corollary 3.3 further in the case of residually rationally solvable groups. Let GG be a group. If RR is any ring, denote by

GR(i)=ker⁡(GR(i−1)→H1​(GR(i−1),R))G^{(i)}_{R}=\ker\left(G^{(i-1)}_{R}\to H_{1}\left(G^{(i-1)}_{R},R\right)\right)

the ithi^{\text{th}} term of the RR-derived series, where GR(0)=GG^{(0)}_{R}=G. A group GG is RR-solvable if GR(n)=1G_{R}^{(n)}=1 for some nn and is residually RR-solvable if ⋂i=0∞GR(i)=1\bigcap_{i=0}^{\infty}G_{R}^{(i)}=1. Note that GG is residually RR-solvable then it is also fully residually RR-solvable since being RR-solvable is closed under subdirect products. The derived series is the ℤ\mathbb{Z}-derived series and the rational derived series is the ℚ\mathbb{Q}-derived series defined above, a fact we shall use often in the proof of Theorem 1.1. Before embarking on the proof, we first deduce the consequences from the introduction.

Proof of Corollary 1.2.

(2) implies (1) since free groups are residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable (in fact, they are residually torsion-free nilpotent by a result of Magnus [Mag35]) and a {residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable}-by-{ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable} group is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable. (1) implies (2) by Corollary 3.3. (3) implies (1) by Theorem 1.1. Finally, if GG is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable, then Theorem 1.1 implies that for any r∈Fr\in F and k⩾1k\geqslant 1 such that w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle], we must have that ⟨⟨r⟩⟩G=1\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G}=1 (since ⟨⟨r⟩⟩G\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G} is ℚ\mathbb{Q}-perfect) and so ⟨⟨w⟩⟩=⟨⟨r⟩⟩\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle=\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle. The fact that ww must then be conjugate to rr or r−1r^{-1} is a theorem of Magnus [Mag30]. ∎

We may now prove the first part of Corollary 1.3.

Corollary 4.1.

Torsion-free positive one-relator groups are free-by-(ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable) and so are residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable.

Proof.

Let FF be a free group, S⊂FS\subset F a free basis and w∈Fw\in F a cyclically reduced word that is positive over SS. Let r∈Fr\in F be a cyclically reduced element and let k⩾1k\geqslant 1 be such that w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle]. Let XX be a presentation complex for F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle. Let Y→XY\to X be the cover corresponding to the subgroup ⟨⟨r⟩⟩⊲F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩=π1​(X)\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle\triangleleft F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle=\pi_{1}(X) and let λ:S1→Y\lambda\colon S^{1}\to Y be the cycle labelled by ww (at a chosen basepoint). By Theorem 3.1, the cycle ρ:S1→Y\rho\colon S^{1}\to Y labelled by rr is embedded. Let C⊂YC\subset Y be the image of ρ\rho. By definition of rr, we have that [λ]=[ρ]k[\lambda]=[\rho]^{k} as elements of Z1​(Y,ℤ)Z_{1}(Y,\mathbb{Z}). But since ww is positive, [λ][\lambda] is a sum of 1-cells, one for each 1-cell that λ\lambda traverses, and each with coefficient +1+1. Since these 1-cells must be precisely the 1-cells in CC, this implies λ\lambda is supported in CC. Since ww is not a proper power, this means that k=1k=1 and w=rw=r. Now Corollary 1.2 implies that F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable. ∎

Although one-relator groups with torsion cannot be residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable, we may use the canonical torsion-free quotient to establish residual solvability in some cases.

Lemma 4.2.

Let FF be a free group, let w∈Fw\in F be an element that is not a proper power and let n⩾2n\geqslant 2 be an integer. If F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable, then F/⟨⟨wn⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle w^{n}\rangle\!\rangle is residually solvable.

Proof.

If F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable, there is a homomorphism F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩→QF/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle\to Q to a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable group QQ such that each proper non-empty subword of ww is non-trivial in the image. Composing the epimorphism F/⟨⟨wn⟩⟩→F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle w^{n}\rangle\!\rangle\to F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle, we obtain a homomorphism F/⟨⟨wn⟩⟩→QF/\langle\!\langle w^{n}\rangle\!\rangle\to Q with kernel a free product of a free group and copies of ℤ/n​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} by Theorem 3.2. Since this kernel is residually solvable, F/⟨⟨wn⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle w^{n}\rangle\!\rangle is residually solvable. ∎

Using Lemma 4.2 we may complete the proof of Corollary 1.3.

Corollary 4.3.

Positive one-relator groups are free-by-solvable and so are residually solvable.

The following is a slightly expanded version of Corollary 1.4 from the introduction.

Corollary 4.4.

There is an algorithm that, on input a word ww over an alphabet S⊔S−1S\sqcup S^{-1}, computes an element rr which normally generates Gℚ(ω)G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(\omega)}, where G=F⁡(S)/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F(S)/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle, and moreover, decides whether GG is residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable.

Proof.

We first show that given a word rr over SS, we can decide whether there is some k⩾1k\geqslant 1 such that w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle]. The word problem for one-relator groups is decidable by a result of Magnus [Mag32]. Hence, we can compute arbitrarily large balls in the Cayley graph for F⁡(S)/⟨⟨r⟩⟩F(S)/\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle. Computing the ball B⁡(|w|)B(|w|) of radius |w||w| in the Cayley graph, to conclude the (sub)procedure we simply need to determine whether the chain in C1​(B​(|w|))C_{1}(B(|w|)) determined by ww is equal to a multiple of the cycle determined by rr in C1​(B​(|w|))C_{1}(B(|w|)), which is certainly decidable.

Now we enumerate all words rr of length bounded above by that of ww and use the above procedure to determine whether w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle] or not. For each such rr, the subgroup ⟨⟨r⟩⟩G\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G} is ℚ\mathbb{Q}-perfect (as remarked in the introduction). Since the maximal ℚ\mathbb{Q}-perfect subgroup of GG is unique, there will be some such rr such that all others lie in ⟨⟨r⟩⟩\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle. Since membership in ⟨⟨r⟩⟩\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle is decidable by [Mag32], we may find the rr that generates the maximal ℚ\mathbb{Q}-perfect subgroup of GG. Finally, by Corollary 1.2, to determine whether ⟨⟨r⟩⟩G=1\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G}=1, we simply need to check whether ww is conjugate to rr or r−1r^{-1}. ∎

We now turn to the proof of Theorem 1.1. We shall first need a simple, yet critical, lemma. Recall that if RR is a ring, the group ring R​GRG is the ring with elements the formal sums r=∑g∈Grg⋅gr=\sum_{g\in G}r_{g}\cdot g where rg∈Rr_{g}\in R and rg≠0r_{g}\neq 0 for all but finitely many elements. The support of the element rr in the group ring R​GRG is defined as the set

supp⁡(r)={g∈G∣rg≠0}⊂G.\supp(r)=\{g\in G\mid r_{g}\neq 0\}\subset G.

Note that supp⁡(r​s)⊂supp⁡(r)​supp⁡(s)\supp(rs)\subset\supp(r)\supp(s) for all r,s∈R​Gr,s\in RG.

Lemma 4.5.

Let GG be locally indicable, let RR be a domain and let 0≠a,b∈R​G0\neq a,b\in RG. Then supp⁡(a​b)⊂supp⁡(b)\supp(ab)\subset\supp(b) if and only if supp⁡(a)=1\supp(a)=1.

Proof.

Suppose for a contradiction that supp⁡(a)≠1\supp(a)\neq 1, but that supp⁡(a​b)⊂supp⁡(b)\supp(ab)\subset\supp(b). If 1∉supp⁡(a)1\notin\supp(a), then supp⁡((a+1)​b)⊂supp⁡(b)\supp((a+1)b)\subset\supp(b), so by possibly replacing aa with a+1a+1, we may assume that 1∈supp⁡(a)1\in\supp(a). In particular, |supp⁡(a)|⩾2|\supp(a)|\geqslant 2. If g1​h1∈supp⁡(b)g_{1}h_{1}\in\supp(b), then g1⋅h1=1⋅(g1​h1)g_{1}\cdot h_{1}=1\cdot(g_{1}h_{1}) implies that g1=1g_{1}=1. Similarly for g2​h2g_{2}h_{2}. Since g1≠g2g_{1}\neq g_{2}, this implies that either g1​h1∉supp⁡(b)g_{1}h_{1}\notin\supp(b) or g2​h2∉supp⁡(b)g_{2}h_{2}\notin\supp(b). But this is a contradiction and so supp⁡(a)=1\supp(a)=1. ∎

Example 4.6.

Consider the one-relator group

G=⟨a,b∣[a[[a,b],[b,a−1]],b]⟩.G=\langle a,b\mid[a[[a,b],[b,a^{-1}]],b]\rangle.

We may re-express this relator as

[a⁡[[a,b],[b,a−1]],b]\displaystyle[a[[a,b],[b,a^{-1}]],b] =[a⁡[[a,b],[a,b]a],b]\displaystyle=[a[[a,b],[a,b]^{a}],b]
=[a,b]​([[a,b],[a,b]a]b​a−1​b−1​([[a,b],[a,b]a]−1)a−1​b−1)\displaystyle=[a,b]\left([[a,b],[a,b]^{a}]^{ba^{-1}b^{-1}}\left([[a,b],[a,b]^{a}]^{-1}\right)^{a^{-1}b^{-1}}\right)

and so Gℚ(ω)=Gℚ(1)=⟨⟨[a,b]⟩⟩GG_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(\omega)}=G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(1)}=\langle\!\langle[a,b]\rangle\!\rangle_{G}. Hence, GG is not residually ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable and its abelianisation is its maximal ℚ\mathbb{Q}-solvable quotient. In fact, since Gℚ(1)G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(1)} is perfect, GG is not residually solvable either.

4.1. The derived series

We suspect the same results proved in this article should hold for the usual derived series of one-relator groups. Unfortunately, local indicability of the successive quotients was essential for our proofs. Following a suggestion of Jens Harlander, we may show that there is one case in which our result applies to the derived series.

Corollary 4.7.

Let G=F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle be a one-relator group with H2​(G)=0H^{2}(G)=0. There is a word r∈Fr\in F such that w∈r⁡[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle] and

G(ω+1)=G(ω)=⟨⟨r⟩⟩G.G^{(\omega+1)}=G^{(\omega)}=\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G}.

In particular, the maximal residually solvable quotient of GG is the one-relator group F/⟨⟨r⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle.

Proof.

If G=F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle is a one-relator group with H2​(G)=0H^{2}(G)=0, we have that H2​(G)=0H_{2}(G)=0 and H1​(G)H_{1}(G) is torsion-free by Lyndon’s identity theorem [Lyn50]. Hence, GG is an EE-group in the sense of Strebel and so we may apply [Str74, Theorem A] to conclude that G(α)=Gℚ(α)G^{(\alpha)}=G_{\mathbb{Q}}^{(\alpha)} for all ordinals α\alpha. By Theorem 1.1, there is a word r∈Fr\in F and k⩾1k\geqslant 1 such that G(ω)=⟨⟨r⟩⟩GG^{(\omega)}=\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G} and such that w∈rk​[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r^{k}[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle]. Since H2​(G)=0H_{2}(G)=0, we have that rkr^{k} is non-trivial in the abelianisation of FF. Since H1​(G)H_{1}(G) is torsion-free, rr is not a proper power in the abelianisation of H1​(G)H_{1}(G) and so k=1k=1. ∎

We conclude with a conjecture.

Conjecture 4.8.

Let G=F/⟨⟨w⟩⟩G=F/\langle\!\langle w\rangle\!\rangle be a one-relator group. There is a word r∈Fr\in F such that w∈r⁡[⟨⟨r⟩⟩,⟨⟨r⟩⟩]w\in r[\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle,\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle] and

G(ω+1)=G(ω)=⟨⟨r⟩⟩G.G^{(\omega+1)}=G^{(\omega)}=\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle_{G}.

In particular, the maximal residually solvable quotient of GG is the one-relator group F/⟨⟨r⟩⟩F/\langle\!\langle r\rangle\!\rangle.
